newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt pledges improved conditions for gypsies.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt pledges improved conditions for gypsies.

text.p: The Czech government on Thursday promised to adopt measures to improve living conditions for the country's gypsies, after a television report prompted hundreds of them to flood Canadian embassies to seek asylum across the Atlantic.

Speaking after a meeting with gypsy leaders on Thursday, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said the government in the coming weeks would discuss long-standing problems in the gypsy community, including questions of employment, housing and discrimination.
"I think everyone believes that the situation is very unfortunate, very unsafe and both sides have an interest to solve it," he said.

Over the past week, Czech gypsies have flocked to Canadian embassies in Prague and Vienna after a local television report showed a gypsy family living comfortably in Canada while its case for asylum was considered.

Gypsy leaders hailed Klaus's announcement as a step in the right direction, and also warned members of their community to stay put after hundreds reportedly sold all of their property to buy plane tickets to Canada.
"We have a good feeling about today's meeting with Mr. Klaus," gypsy leader Emil Scuka said after the meeting.

Officials at Canada's embassy in Prague said the report gave gypsies the false impression that upon arriving in Canada they would receive money and accommodation, and that their chance of getting refugee status was very high.
Czech citizens are not required to have a visa to visit Canada although they must show a return ticket when entering and prove they have the means to finance their stay.

Ottawa's Prague embassy said on Thursday it was continuing to receive calls -- though far fewer than the hundreds daily it was inundated with immediately after the report -- mostly from Czech gypsies in the eastern city of Ostrava who mistakenly thought Canada had a special asylum programme for them.
Canada has no special programme for Czech gypsies. It follows the United Nations convention on refugees.

The reaction to the report shown on the commercial station TV Nova last Thursday has grown into a heated debate in the media over attitudes toward the large and relatively poor Czech gypsy population.

Czech politicians have long wrestled with accusations by human rights campaigners and western governments that the country gives unfair treatment to its gypsies, who are estimated to total in the hundreds of thousands.
Gypsies have often been the target of violent racially motivated attacks, and there is a widespread belief that they are responsible for much of the country's crime.
"The programme which the government wants to adopt, and which the Prime Minister has promised, will be positive also for the Czech public and will soon ease racial discrimination," Scuka added.
